speaker: SPEAKER_00
transcript: This is AgriPulse Open Mike. I'm your host Jeff Alley. Our guest this week is Oklahoma 3rd District Representative Frank Lucas. AgriPulse Open Mike is brought to you by the American Sugar Alliance. The American Sugar Alliance is working toward a global subsidy ceasefire. Learn more about the 0-4-0 plan at sugaralliance.org. AgriPulse Open Mike continues with Congressman Frank Lucas. Next, Sugar subsidies in 120 countries are on the rise and threatening 142,000 U.S. jobs. That's why the American Sugar Alliance is pushing for a global subsidy ceasefire. Their goal is a subsidy-free world market that fosters efficiency, and they know that unilateral disarmament of America's no-cost policy without concessions from abroad will only outsource U.S. jobs and reward foreign subsidizers. Their plan is to call this zero for zero sugar policy, and you can learn more at sugaralliance.org. This is AgriPulse Open Mike. Born in Oklahoma and representing the fifth generation of his family's livestock and crop farming operation, Representative Frank Lucas is a steadfast soldier for agriculture on Capitol Hill. Lucas says the legislature made significant progress on the nation's finances before leaving town for the August break, but he says there's still some very heavy lifting ahead when congressional leaders return in September.

speaker: SPEAKER_01
transcript: I am an internal optimist, Jeff. I wouldn't be a wheat farmer in Oklahoma by real profession. Bottom line is this. I have a difficult time seeing how with the Mexicans having ratified their version or their part of the treaty, with the Canadians on the verge of ratifying their part of the treaty, I have a hard time seeing how you go in and really renegotiate. Now, maybe there'll be some side agreements, maybe there'll be some understandings, but I would hope Speaker Pelosi is more focused on getting U.S. goods into the world market again, especially in Canada and Mexico than being focused, shall we say, on preventing the president from having a win, because with the ratification of U.S. MCA, that's the first big step because those are our huge trading partners to the North and South. You succeed that, that puts huge pressure on Europeans, that puts huge pressure on the Japanese to come to terms. You bring those trade agreements to focus, then at least the proverbial 12,000 ton economic grille out there, how we deal with the Chinese, with agreements negotiated and ratified with everybody but them. That puts incredible pressure on them to come to terms with, because remember the Chinese have no particular perspective about ratifying this, because for the last 25, 30 years they have sold us literally two or three times more stuff than they bought from us. We have provided the capital to create their industrial economy. There's even rumors that perhaps the Chinese goal is to drag on the negotiations long enough to enable a change in administration and they would get better terms from a different president than they'll get from Donald Trump. I hope those things are all wrong. But I know if we can't ratify USMCA, if we can't bring things to focus here in our immediate neighborhood, North and South and North America, and how in the world will we bring the rest of this to a conclusion? And I guess I tell, if I remind people in my town meetings across the district, when it comes to agricultural products, grain, meat, whatever, from the beginning of the country, we have been exporters. We have always produced more than we can consume in almost every commodity group. We have to sell into the world markets. This prevailing in the international trade negotiations to get a more equitable situation means life or death for us in the long haul. So President Trump is right. I hope the Speaker will put the economic interest to the country ahead of short-term politics, but it's going to be a while September, Jim.
